extracted.intended_audience: NLP / multimodal ML researchers, dataset builders, and researchers studying computational humor
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating benchmarks/tasks that test AI models' ability to 'understand' sophisticated multimodal humor (New Yorker cartoon captions) using vision-and-language and language-only setups, with rich annotations (entities, unusualness, joke explanations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding sophisticated multimodal humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers evaluate AI models' ability to understand sophisticated multimodal humor in The New Yorker Caption Contest using vision-and-language and language-only models, finding performance gaps compared to humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The benchmark's goal is to 'demonstrate understanding' of New Yorker-caliber cartoons—i.e., humor that arises from subtle, multimodal interactions between image and caption and from cultural and experiential allusions. Models are expected to handle the sophistication characteristic of these cartoons rather than only surface-level features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grasping complex and unexpected image-caption relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks are 'carefully circumscribed' such that it suffices (but is not necessary) to grasp potentially complex and unexpected relationships between image and caption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should measure whether a model captures how the image and caption interact (e.g., irony, juxtaposition, role reversal) rather than treating text and image independently. The tasks are constructed so understanding these relationships is sufficient for success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing complex and unexpected allusions to human experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks require grasping 'complex and unexpected allusions to the wide varieties of human experience'; such allusions are hallmarks of a New Yorker-caliber cartoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models must handle cultural, situational, and experiential references and infer implicit background knowledge; evaluation should account for these kinds of allusive comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the joke
rubrics_metrics.description: The released corpora include annotations ... and an explanation of the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One evaluation target is producing (or matching) a human-like explanation of why a caption is funny given the image—i.e., articulating the mechanism of the humor. Scoring can compare model explanations to annotated human explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify image locations/entities
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models should be able to detect and name salient objects, people, and locations in the cartoon as part of understanding context relevant to the joke; evaluations may use these labeled entities as gold targets or inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what's unusual about the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotations describe 'what's unusual about the scene.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key rubric is detecting anomalous or unexpected elements in the image that contribute to the humor (e.g., absurd object placement, incongruous behavior). Models should pinpoint such unusual aspects; scoring can compare identified unusualness to annotator labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare vision-and-language and language-only approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: The study investigates vision-and-language models that take as input the cartoon pixels and caption directly, as well as language-only models for which we circumvent image-processing by providing textual descriptions of the image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should consider both modalities: direct pixel+text models and models given textual scene descriptions. Comparisons illuminate what is lost/gained by removing raw visual input and whether language-only aids via descriptive prompts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure performance gaps relative to humans
rubrics_metrics.description: Even with the rich multifaceted annotations we provide for the cartoon images, we identify performance gaps between high-quality machine learning models (e.g., a fine-tuned, 175B parameter language model) and humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmarks should include human baselines and quantify gaps (accuracy, explanation quality, etc.). Use human performance as an upper-bound reference when judging model adequacy for 'understanding' humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of carefully circumscribed tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: We develop three carefully circumscribed tasks for which it suffices (but is not necessary) to grasp potentially complex ... relationships ... and allusions ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Task design itself is a rubric: tasks should be narrowly scoped so success reasonably maps to the targeted notion of understanding (e.g., targeted probes rather than open-ended generation). Provide clear task definitions and evaluation protocols to ensure interpretability of what 'understanding' entails.
